chiral-theory.title: Chiral Theory and the Standard Model
chiral-theory.content:
The asymmetric transformation of left- and right-handed fermion fields under the gauge groups of the Standard Model establishes the fundamental chirality that underlies weak interactions and parity violation in particle physics. Unlike classical vector fields whose strengths are characterized by The Electromagnetic Field Strength Tensor (\( F^{\mu\nu} \)), fermions are represented by Dirac spinors whose left- and right-handed components transform under completely different representations of the gauge group. This chiral asymmetry is responsible for the violation of CP symmetry, which is essential for explaining the observed imbalance between baryonic matter and antimatter in the cosmos, a cosmological problem analyzed in Matter-Antimatter Asymmetry and Baryogenesis. In a chiral theory, the left-handed fermions exist as doublets under weak isospin, whereas the right-handed fermions exist as singlets, preventing any standard Dirac mass term from being gauge-invariant without the introduction of a spontaneously broken scalar Higgs field.

The mathematical definition of these left- and right-handed projection operators and their corresponding gauge-covariant field dynamics is formulated using the Dirac gamma matrices. The mathematical statement of this chiral structure is given by the chiral projection and left-right covariant field relations, written as:

\[ \psi_{L,R} = \frac{1 \mp \gamma_5}{2}\psi, \quad \mathcal{L}_{\text{chiral}} = i\bar{\psi}_L \gamma^\mu D_\mu \psi_L + i\bar{\psi}_R \gamma^\mu D_\mu \psi_R \]
where \( \psi \) represents the four-component Dirac spinor field, \( \gamma_5 = i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3 \) is the chiral Dirac matrix, and \( P_{L,R} = (1 \mp \gamma_5)/2 \) are the left- and right-handed projection operators. The kinetic terms are governed by the chiral Lagrangian \( \mathcal{L}_{\text{chiral}} \), where \( \gamma^\mu \) are the standard Dirac matrices and \( D_\mu \) is the gauge-covariant derivative. Because the covariant derivative \( D_\mu \) contains different gauge fields and coupling constants for the left- and right-handed components—specifically coupling the left-handed doublets to the \( SU(2)_L \) weak gauge fields while leaving the right-handed singlets uncoupled—the left and right fields exhibit completely decoupled gauge dynamics in the kinetic sector.

The four-dimensional coordinate system that supports these spinor fields is defined over a flat spacetime manifold equipped with Minkowski Metric, which defines the causal light-cone boundaries and constrains the propagation of relativistic waves. The experimental signature of this chiral coupling was historically discovered through the analysis of weak decays, which are governed by The V-A (Vector minus Axial-vector) Interaction, reflecting the absolute preference of the weak force for left-handed particles and right-handed antiparticles. This chiral structure is unified under the framework of Electroweak Symmetry Group (SU(2)L x U(1)Y), which groups the left-handed fermions into weak isospin doublets and the right-handed fermions into hypercharge singlets, requiring that the electroweak gauge bosons couple only to the left-handed currents in the weak sector.

The physical consequences of this chiral gauge coupling are reflected in the macroscopic behaviors of quantum ensembles, which are analyzed under the framework of Statistical Distribution of Quantum Outcomes to determine the probability distributions of scattering cross-sections and decay rates. Because the chiral currents are asymmetric, the conservation of the axial current is broken by quantum anomalies at the loop level, providing a non-perturbative mechanism for generating baryon and lepton number violations in the early universe. This anomalous decay of chiral charges is critical for understanding the non-equilibrium transitions that occurred during the electroweak phase transition, showing how the algebraic chiral structures of quantum field theory propagate up to dictate the macroscopic matter content of the modern universe.

The physical meaning of this chiral theory exhibits an elegant limiting case when we analyze the behavior of the system in the high-energy regime where the fermion mass \( m \) is completely negligible compared to the system's energy scale. In this massless limit \( m \to 0 \), the chirality of a particle becomes a strictly conserved quantum number that is identical to its physical helicity, representing the projection of its spin along its direction of motion. Under these ultra-relativistic conditions, the left- and right-handed fermion spinor components decouple completely in the Lagrangian, and the global chiral symmetry of the theory is fully restored. Conversely, the introduction of a non-zero mass couples the left- and right-handed components, allowing for chiral transitions and providing a direct measure of the spontaneous breaking of electroweak symmetry by the vacuum expectation value of the Higgs field.

chandrasekhar-limit.title: Chandrasekhar Limit
chandrasekhar-limit.content:
The gravitational stability of a highly evolved stellar core that has exhausted its thermonuclear fuel depends entirely on the quantum-mechanical pressure exerted by degenerate electrons. For compact objects such as white dwarfs, this outward pressure counteracts the inward pull of gravity, maintaining a stable equilibrium without requiring any thermal energy generation. The observational mapping of these stellar remnants across cosmic distances is calibrated using standard candles, including the Cepheid variables characterized by Leavitt's Law (Period-Luminosity Relationship), which establishes the absolute distance scale of nearby galaxies. In the event that a white dwarf exceeds its stable mass boundary, it undergoes a thermonuclear runaway explosion, generating a Type Ia supernova. The gravitational waves produced by subsequent compact object mergers are detected with high precision by LIGO: Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, providing independent constraints on the cosmic distance scale and the properties of highly dense matter. These gravitational-wave observations offer direct insights into the final stages of stellar collapse, permitting astrophysicists to model the extreme dynamics of merging remnants under intense gravitational fields.

The maximum mass that such a degenerate stellar core can support before gravitational forces overcome the quantum-mechanical pressure is determined by the transition of the degenerate electrons into the ultra-relativistic regime. The mathematical statement of this limiting mass is given by the relativistic degeneracy mass limit relation, written as:

\[ M_{\text{Ch}} = \frac{3\sqrt{2\pi}}{8} \left( \frac{\hbar c}{G} \right)^{3/2} \left( \frac{1}{\mu_e m_H} \right)^2 \approx 1.4 M_\odot \]
where \( M_{\text{Ch}} \) represents the Chandrasekhar limit, \( \hbar \) is the reduced Planck's constant, \( c \) is the speed of light, \( G \) is the gravitational constant, \( \mu_e \) is the mean molecular weight per electron (typically equal to 2 for carbon-oxygen white dwarfs), \( m_H \) is the mass of a hydrogen atom, and \( M_\odot \) represents the solar mass. In this formulation, the limit is independent of the stellar radius, arising from a balance where both the self-gravitational pressure and the ultra-relativistic degeneracy pressure scale as the four-thirds power of the density. Consequently, if the mass of the core exceeds this mathematical threshold, no increase in density can generate sufficient pressure to halt the collapse, triggering a runaway contraction into a neutron star or black hole.

The microphysical origin of this pressure is rooted in the relativistic energy spectrum of degenerate fermions, which is governed on a microscopic scale by The Energy-Momentum Relation, relating particle energy to momentum and invariant rest mass. On an astrophysical scale, the macroscopic geometry of this gravitational collapse is described by the equations of General Relativity in Astrophysics and Cosmology, which model the curvature of spacetime manifolds around highly dense matter distributions. In the historical development of physical cosmology, these stellar collapse limits were analyzed alongside global cosmological models, including The Einstein-de Sitter Universe (\(\Omega_m = 1\)), which describes a flat, matter-dominated universe with zero cosmological constant. By comparing the local degeneracy pressure of stellar cores with the global gravitational expansion of the universe, astrophysicists can map the flow of energy and matter across curved spacetime manifolds, establishing the Chandrasekhar limit as a fundamental benchmark in stellar evolution. This comparison relies on modelling the white dwarf as a relativistic polytrope with index n=3, where the equation of state transitions from non-relativistic to ultra-relativistic regimes as the density climbs towards the center of the star.

The physical behavior of these degenerate stellar cores exhibits an important limiting case when the mass of the core is well below the Chandrasekhar limit. In this non-relativistic limit where \( M \ll M_{\text{Ch}} \), the Fermi momentum of the degenerate electrons remains much smaller than their rest mass energy, a regime where the electron degeneracy pressure scales as the five-thirds power of the density. Under these conditions, the stellar core is stably supported by non-relativistic degeneracy pressure, and the core's radius exhibits a stable, inverse scaling relation where the radius decreases as the mass increases, \( R \propto M^{-1/3} \). As the stellar mass increases toward the relativistic limit, the electrons are driven into the ultra-relativistic regime where their velocity approaches the speed of light \( c \). This transition is crucial for understanding how the core's behavior diverges from classical polytropic models, culminating in the accelerated expansion of the modern universe where the global dynamics are eventually dominated by dark energy, as represented by The De Sitter Universe (\(\Omega_\Lambda = 1\)).

jeans-mass.title: Jeans Mass
jeans-mass.content:
The fragmentation of giant molecular clouds and the subsequent initiation of star formation are governed by the balance between internal thermal pressure and self-gravitational attraction. When a gas cloud's mass exceeds a critical threshold, the inward pull of gravity overcomes the outward pressure forces, triggering a runaway gravitational collapse. The physical properties of these star-forming regions and their distance metrics are calibrated using classical distance ladders, including the period-luminosity relation of Cepheid variables known as Leavitt's Law (Period-Luminosity Relationship). Over much longer timescales, the endpoint of this stellar evolution leads to the formation of compact stellar remnants whose violent mergers generate gravitational waves. These ripples in spacetime are detected by LIGO: Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, providing independent constraints on the equation of state of highly dense matter and the history of cosmic star formation.

The mathematical boundary that separates stable acoustic oscillations from runaway gravitational collapse is determined by the Jeans instability criterion. The mathematical statement of this critical mass threshold is given by the Jeans mass collapse threshold relation, written as:

\[ M_J = \frac{\pi^{5/2}}{6 G^{3/2}} \frac{c_s^3}{\sqrt{\rho_0}} \]
where \( M_J \) represents the Jeans mass, \( G \) is the gravitational constant, \( c_s = \sqrt{\gamma k_B T / m} \) is the adiabatic sound speed of the gas (with \( \gamma \) being the adiabatic index, \( k_B \) being the Boltzmann constant, \( T \) being the temperature, and \( m \) being the mean molecular mass), and \( \rho_0 \) represents the unperturbed background mass density of the gas cloud. In this formulation, the Jeans mass scales as the cube of the sound speed and is inversely proportional to the square root of the density. This means that hotter, less dense gas clouds require a much larger mass to initiate collapse, whereas cold, dense regions can easily fragment into smaller, stellar-sized cores.

The microphysical propagation of energy and momentum within these collapsing gas clouds is constrained by the relativistic energy spectrum of the gas particles, which is governed by The Energy-Momentum Relation, relating particle energy to momentum and invariant rest mass. On a cosmological scale, these local collapse dynamics occurred within the expanding background of the early universe, a process historically modeled by The Einstein-de Sitter Universe (\(\Omega_m = 1\)), which describes a flat, matter-dominated universe with zero cosmological constant. In this expanding matter-dominated background, the growth rate of density perturbations is suppressed from exponential to power-law growth, demonstrating how the global cosmic expansion rate counteracts the local self-gravitational instability.

The mathematical derivation of this instability is performed by linearizing the fundamental fluid equations—the continuity equation, the Euler equation, and the Poisson equation for gravity—about a uniform background state. On a macroscopic scale, this linearized analysis is formulated using the equations of General Relativity in Astrophysics and Cosmology, which govern the behavior of curved spacetime manifolds around dense mass distributions. By introducing small density perturbations of the form \( \delta \rho \propto e^{i(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x} - \omega t)} \), physicists can derive a dispersion relation that relates the perturbation frequency to the wavevector. This dispersion relation reveals that if the perturbation wavelength exceeds the Jeans length, the frequency becomes imaginary, transforming the stable acoustic wave into an exponentially growing mode that drives runaway gravitational collapse.

In the modern cosmological epoch, this gravitational instability is analyzed within a multi-component universe where the global expansion rate is dominated by dark energy, as represented by The De Sitter Universe (\(\Omega_\Lambda = 1\)). In this vacuum-dominated regime, the exponential expansion of the cosmic scale factor freezes out the growth of large-scale structure, preventing the formation of new galaxy clusters. Consequently, the Jeans mass in the intergalactic medium increases rapidly, demonstrating how the global dark energy density alters the local collapse thresholds of baryonic matter across cosmological timescales.

The physical behavior of these gaseous perturbations exhibits an important limiting case when the mass of the gas cloud is much smaller than the Jeans mass. In this small-scale limit where \( M \ll M_J \), or equivalently when the perturbation wavelength is much shorter than the Jeans length \( \lambda \ll \lambda_J \), the thermal pressure forces within the gas dominate over the self-gravitational attraction. Under these high-pressure conditions, the self-gravitational term in the dispersion relation becomes completely negligible, and the density perturbation propagates harmlessly through the medium as a stable acoustic wave traveling at the sound speed \( c_s \). As the gas cloud cools, the sound speed decreases, causing the Jeans mass to drop until the cloud's mass exceeds the threshold, triggering the transition from stable wave propagation to gravitational collapse.
